newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian forces slowly close in on opposition.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian forces slowly close in on opposition.

text.p: Cambodian government troops on Friday cautiously advanced to within 12 km (seven miles) of O'Smach, the last major town held by forces loyal to ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, witnesses said.

At the front line near Phong, a small village with a handful of modest huts, very light, sporadic shelling from both sides was heard throughout the day, with more than an hour elapsing between most exchanges.

The government army's progress north toward O'Smach, 12 km (seven miles) north of Phong, was severely hampered by blown out bridges, landmines and the beginning of the troops' approach into thick jungle, military officials said. Since Thursday the army had advanced three km, they said.
Two royalist soldiers were dead by the road to O'Smach, and two broken down tanks sat abandoned by retreating royalists.
Government officials said they had taken one royalist prisoner on Friday and two of their own troops had suffered leg injuries. No further casualty information was available.
Several hundred government troops, under the control of powerful Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, have been closing in on O'Smach in recent days to finish off forces loyal to Ranariddh.
Ranariddh, Hun Sen's former partner in a shaky coalition government since 1993, was ousted by Hun Sen on July 6 after two days of fighting in Phnom Penh.
Witnesses said the government troops fighting near Phong belonged to a division controlled by Ranariddh before the coup.

On Thursday Hun Sen said he would order his armed forces to seize O'Smach, a northwestern town near the Thai border, within a day, but it remained in royalist hands as of Friday afternoon, witnesses said. A Reuters correspondent on the Thai side of the border near O'Smach said the area was quiet.
Some 15,000 refugees in the town have been preparing to take refuge in Thailand and would be allowed to cross when the situation warranted it, Thai authorities said.
Witnesses near Phong said the area was devoid of civilians, who had fled, and soldiers were living in village homes.
Both sides in the civil war seem to have ignored a ceasefire call on Friday by the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN).

Thai Foreign Minister Prachuab Chaiyasarn told Ranariddh in Bangkok that an immediate ceasefire in Cambodia was a first priority. But Ranariddh said he would not call a unilateral ceasefire and that he and Hun Sen should meet first.
After his meeting with Prachuab, Ranariddh denied Khmer Rouge radio reports on Friday that its forces had formed a military alliance with the royalist forces in fighting against Hun Sen.
